## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.101992.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.101992.3.sa1)

In this meta-analysis, Ng and colleagues review the association between slow-oscillation spindle coupling during sleep and overnight memory consolidation. The coupling of these oscillations (and also hippocampal sharp-wave ripples) have been central to theories and mechanistic models of active systems consolidation, that posit that the coupling between ripples, spindles, and slow oscillations (SOs) coordinate and drive the coordinated reactivation of memories in hippocampus and cortex, facilitating cross-regional information and ultimately memory strengthening and stabilisation.

Given the importance that these coupling mechanisms have been given in theory, this is a timely and important contribution to the literature in terms of determining whether these theoretical assumptions hold true in human data. The results show that the timing of sleep spindles relative to the SO phase, and the consistency of that timing, predicted overnight memory consolidation in meta-analytic models. The overall amount of coupling events did not show as strong a relationship. Coupling phase in particular was moderated by a number of variables including spindle type (fast, slow), channel location (frontal, central, posterior), age, and memory type. The main takeaway is that fast spindles that consistently couple close to the peak of the SO in frontal channel locations are optimal for memory consolidation, in line with theoretical predictions. These findings will be very useful for future researchers in terms of determining necessary sample sizes to observe coupling - memory relationships, and in the selection and reporting of relevant coupling metrics.

Although the meta-analysis covers the three main coupling metrics that are typically assessed (occurrence, timing, and consistency), the meta-analysis also includes spindle amplitude. This may be confusing to readers, as this is not a measurement of SO-spindle coupling but instead a measurement of spindles in general (which may or may not be coupled).

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.101992.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.101992.3.sa3)

This manuscript presents a meta-analysis of 23 studies, which report 297 effect sizes, on the effect of SO-spindle coupling on memory performance. The analysis has been done with great care, and the results are described in great detail. In particular, there are separate analyses for coupling phase, spindle amplitude, coupling strength (e.g., measured by vector length or modulation index), and coupling percentage (i.e., the percentage of SPs coupled with SOs). The authors conclude that the precision and strength of coupling showed significant correlations with memory retention.

There are two main points where I do not agree with the authors.

First, the authors conclude that "SO-SP coupling should be considered as a general physiological mechanism for memory consolidation". However, the reported effect sizes are smaller than what is typically considered a "small effect" (0.10)

Second, the study implements state-of-the-art Bayesian statistics. While some might see this as a strength, I would argue that it is not. A classical meta-analysis is relatively easy to understand, even for readers with only a limited background in statistics. A Bayesian analysis, on the other hand, introduces a number of subjective choices that render it much less transparent. This becomes obvious in the forest plots. It is not immediately apparent to the reader how the distributions for each study represent the reported effect sizes (gray dots), which makes the analyses unnecessarily opaque. It is commendable that the authors now provide classical forest plots as Figs. S10.1-4.

However, analyses that require a "Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method, [..] with the no-U-turn Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) samplers, [..] with each chain undergoing 12,000 iterations (including 2,000 warm-ups)" for calculating accurate Bayes Factors (BF), and checking its convergence "through graphical posterior predictive checks, [..] trace plots, and [..] Gelman and Rubin Diagnostic", which should then result in something resembling "a uniformly undulating wave with high overlap between chains" still seems overly complex. It follows a recent trend in using more and more opaque methods. Where we had to trust published results a decade ago because the data were not openly available, today we must trust the results because methods (including open source software toolboxes) can no longer be checked with reasonable effort.

results.result: The meta-analysis included 23 studies with 297 effect sizes, comprising 730 participants with an average age of 24.8 years (range 7.3-78.0), 49.5% female representation, and average sample size of 31.7 participants per study. Studies included 17 overnight and 6 nap studies measuring 19 declarative and 6 procedural memory tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C48-C52 provide descriptive statistics about the meta-analysis dataset that are internally consistent and clearly reported. These are straightforward data summaries with no analytical concerns.

results.result: Precise and strong SO-fast SP coupling in the frontal lobe predicts memory consolidation, with very strong evidence supporting a small-sized association between preferred coupling phase and memory consolidation (rz,pooled = 0.07 [0.01, 0.13], BF10 = 58.35, probability = 0.98).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C53, C82, C114, C115 present the primary finding with appropriate statistical evidence from Bayesian meta-analysis. The effect size is small but statistically robust with strong Bayes factor support and no publication bias detected (C90). The conclusion is appropriately qualified given the small effect size.

results.result: The association between SO-fast SP coupling and memory consolidation is moderated by age, memory type, cortical area, and SP frequency. Each ten-year increase in age is associated with a 0.06 decrease in effect size, with stronger associations observed in young adults, frontal regions, fast spindles, and declarative memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C83, C55, C101, C118 report moderator analyses with appropriate statistical support. The age effect shows strong evidence (BF10 = 160.94), and the pattern of stronger effects in specific subgroups is consistent across multiple moderators. However, the limited number of studies on children and older adults (acknowledged in C101) introduces some uncertainty about developmental effects.

results.result: There is a considerable spatiotemporal shift in preferred coupling phase from frontal to posterior regions, with frontal areas showing phase around 0.13 rad [0.00, 0.27] (closest to SO peak), central at -0.27 rad [-0.37, -0.18], and posterior at -0.41 rad [-0.54, -0.27]. Frontal coupling shows the strongest association with memory consolidation and a significant quadratic phase-memory relationship.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63, C93-C95, C97 present spatiotemporal analysis findings with extremely strong statistical evidence (BF10 = +∞ for regional differences). The Bayesian circular mixed-effects model appropriately accounts for repeated measurements. The quadratic relationship in frontal regions (C95) is supported by Figure 5A showing r=0.26, p<0.01. This represents a novel contribution to the field.

results.result: SP amplitude shows high variability in its association with memory consolidation. Only fast SP amplitude in frontal regions and hippocampal-dependent memory shows strong evidence of association. The precision and strength of SO-SP coupling are more crucial indicators than SP amplitude alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69, C71, C84-C87, C116 present findings on SP amplitude with appropriate caveats about variability. The overall model shows moderate evidence (BF10 = 8.28) but wide credible intervals. The comparison with prior meta-analyses (C84) is appropriate. The conclusion that coupling measures are more predictive than amplitude alone (C87) is supported by comparing effect sizes across analyses, though this is an inference rather than direct statistical comparison.

results.result: Mean SO-fast SP coupling strength measured by mean vector length is 0.33 [0.27, 0.39], while SO-slow SP coupling strength is 0.23 [0.19, 0.27]. Mean SO-fast SP coupling percentage is 21.17 [15.95, 26.39]%, while SO-slow SP coupling percentage is 24.07 [17.59, 30.56]%.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76, C79-C80 provide descriptive statistics for coupling measures. These are straightforward data summaries with credible intervals reported. The values are consistent with the ranges expected from the literature.

results.result: The phase and strength of coupling between fast SPs and SOs retain strong predictive ability for memory retention in most moderator subgroups, with similar results not observed for slow SPs. No publication bias was detected for coupling phase and strength analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 summarize robustness findings across moderator analyses. The lack of publication bias is supported by Egger's regression (p=0.59) and rank correlation test (p=0.52) for phase, and similar tests for strength. The differential findings for fast vs. slow SPs are consistent across multiple analyses.

results.result: The coupling phase has widespread predictive role for both declarative and procedural memory, while coupling strength only correlates with hippocampus-dependent memory. Region-specific associations exist with declarative memory in frontal lobe and procedural memory in motor cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 present memory type moderation findings. However, the authors acknowledge limited effect sizes for emotional (k=12) and spatial (k=7) tasks, requiring cautious interpretation. The differential findings for phase vs. strength across memory types are interesting but the mechanisms remain unclear. C100 appropriately cites prior work supporting region-specificity.

results.result: Sleep stage and bout conditions did not moderate the coupling-memory association. Co-occurrence rate of SO-SP coupling is higher during SWS compared to N2, but no differences were found between overnight sleep and naps.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 report null findings for stage and bout moderators with appropriate statistical evidence (weak BF10 values). The authors acknowledge this is surprising (C103) and provide a reasonable explanation focusing on precision/strength over prevalence. The nap finding (C105) is consistent with prior meta-analyses (Kumral et al., 2023; Schmid et al., 2020).

results.result: Frontal fast SPs (~10-14 Hz) occur near the up-state peak of frontal-predominant global SOs with lower frequency than centro-parietal fast SPs (~14-17 Hz), while slow SPs occur before the trough of the SO down-state.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 present findings on SP frequency and timing with supporting citations. This addresses confusion in the literature about SP classification and provides evidence for detailed categorization of SP types. The findings are supported by both current data and cited literature (Hahn et al., 2019; Shinomiya et al., 1999; McConnell et al., 2021, 2022).

results.result: Less than half of included studies conducted corrections for multiple comparisons, the majority selectively reported results for significant findings, and only 2 of 23 studies disclosed all processed data and analysis code. However, almost all authors provided data upon request.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 identify methodological limitations in the literature. These are observational findings about the included studies that highlight important issues with reporting practices and reproducibility. The authors' efforts to obtain unreported data (C112) helped mitigate these concerns for the meta-analysis.

results.result: SO-fast SP coupling should be considered as a general physiological mechanism for memory consolidation and can offer more precise predictions within the context of spatiotemporal specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C119 present the main conclusions drawn from the meta-analysis findings. These are supported by the consistent evidence across multiple coupling measures (C115), the robustness across moderator subgroups (C88), and the spatiotemporal specificity findings (C97). However, the small effect sizes (C117) and the inference nature of these conclusions should be noted.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on the active system consolidation theory, neurobiological mechanisms of SO-SP coupling, phase-amplitude coupling concepts, and prior research on moderating factors including memory types, aging, development, and spatiotemporal features.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C47, C91-C92, C96, C102, C113 present background information and prior research findings, all supported by appropriate citations. These establish the theoretical framework and justify the meta-analysis approach. The claims accurately represent cited work and provide necessary context for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: The effect sizes of the main models are relatively small.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 acknowledges that pooled effect sizes are small (rz = 0.07-0.08 for phase and strength). This is an important limitation appropriately noted by the authors. Small effect sizes are common in neuroscience meta-analyses due to complexity and confounding variables, as the authors note.

results.result: The meta-analysis found that precise and strong SO-fast SP coupling in the frontal lobe predicts memory consolidation, with a small but statistically significant association between coupling phase and memory (rz = 0.07, BF10 = 58.35). The authors conclude this represents a general physiological mechanism for memory consolidation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the statistical significance but express concern about the small effect size (~0.5% of variance, r < 0.10). One reviewer explicitly disagrees with the conclusion that SO-SP coupling should be considered 'a general physiological mechanism,' stating the effect sizes are 'smaller than what is typically considered a small effect (0.10).' The editor notes effects are 'limited,' creating uncertainty about the practical significance despite statistical support.

results.result: The meta-analysis identified moderators (age, memory type, cortical area, SP frequency) that modulate the coupling-memory association, with stronger effects in young adults, frontal regions, fast spindles, and declarative memory. Age showed a negative relationship, with each 10-year increase associated with a 0.06 decrease in effect size.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these moderator findings. One reviewer states the results show 'coupling phase in particular was moderated by a number of variables including spindle type (fast, slow), channel location (frontal, central, posterior), age, and memory type,' and another notes the study 'highlighted that co-coupling of SO and the fast SP's phase and amplitude at the frontal part better predicts memory consolidation performance.' The moderator analyses are treated as key contributions.

results.result: Spatiotemporal analysis revealed a phase gradient from frontal to posterior regions, with frontal areas showing preferred coupling phase closest to SO peak (0.13 rad) and strongest association with memory. Only frontal regions showed a significant quadratic phase-memory relationship, supporting spatiotemporal specificity in memory consolidation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these spatiotemporal findings without challenge. One reviewer explicitly notes 'the main takeaway is that fast spindles that consistently couple close to the peak of the SO in frontal channel locations are optimal for memory consolidation, in line with theoretical predictions.' The spatiotemporal specificity is treated as a novel and important contribution to understanding coupling mechanisms.

results.result: The meta-analysis found that SP amplitude-memory associations show high variability, with strong evidence only for fast SP amplitude in frontal regions predicting hippocampal-dependent memory consolidation, not for slow SPs or other conditions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note this finding but express some confusion about its inclusion. One reviewer states 'the meta-analysis also includes spindle amplitude. This may be confusing to readers, as this is not a measurement of SO-spindle coupling but instead a measurement of spindles in general (which may or may not be coupled).' However, the finding itself about variability and specificity is not challenged.

results.result: The coupling phase showed widespread predictive ability for both declarative and procedural memory, while coupling strength only correlated with hippocampus-dependent memory, suggesting different mechanisms for different memory types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these memory-type specific findings. One reviewer notes the results show coupling phase 'predicted overnight memory consolidation in meta-analytic models' and that 'memory type' was among the key moderators. The distinction between phase and strength predictions across memory types is treated as a meaningful finding.

results.result: The meta-analysis found no evidence supporting moderation by sleep stage (N2 vs SWS) or sleep bout (nap vs overnight) on the coupling-memory association, despite higher co-occurrence rates of SO-SP coupling during SWS compared to N2.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these null findings regarding sleep stage and bout moderation. The authors themselves note this is 'somewhat surprising,' but reviewers accept the results as reported without expressing concern about the lack of stage/bout effects.

results.result: The authors conclude that SO-fast SP coupling should be considered a general physiological mechanism for memory consolidation and can offer more precise predictions within spatiotemporal specificity contexts.
results.evaluation: One reviewer explicitly disagrees with this broad conclusion, stating 'the authors conclude that SO-SP coupling should be considered as a general physiological mechanism for memory consolidation. However, the reported effect sizes are smaller than what is typically considered a small effect (0.10).' This directly challenges the claim that the coupling represents a 'general' mechanism given the limited effect sizes.

results.result: The meta-analysis found no publication bias in analyses of coupling phase and strength, reducing likelihood of overestimating true effect sizes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the publication bias assessment. The finding is presented as supporting the validity of the effect size estimates, and reviewers accept this methodological result without comment or concern.

results.result: The meta-analysis identified methodological concerns in the literature: less than half of included studies corrected for multiple comparisons, most studies selectively reported results, and only 2 of 23 studies disclosed all processed data and analysis code.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not dispute these observations about the literature. One reviewer implicitly acknowledges transparency concerns by noting the Bayesian methods 'render it much less transparent' and that 'methods can no longer be checked with reasonable effort,' which aligns with the authors' concerns about data sharing and reporting practices in the field.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on spatiotemporal findings (C61-C63, C93-C95, C97). Both evaluations support these claims as novel contributions showing regional and temporal specificity of SO-SP coupling, with peer reviewers explicitly affirming the frontal fast spindle findings align with theoretical predictions.

Complete agreement on null findings for sleep stage and bout moderators (C103-C105). Both evaluations accept these results without challenge, acknowledging the authors' note that findings are 'somewhat surprising' but treating them as valid.

Significant disagreement on interpretation of primary findings (C4, C53, C82, C114, C115). OpenEval finds claims supported with appropriate qualifications, while peer reviewers express uncertainty about practical significance despite statistical support, with one reviewer explicitly disagreeing that small effect sizes (~0.5% variance) justify calling coupling a 'general physiological mechanism.' OpenEval includes C87 which peer R1 also addresses.

Strong agreement on moderator analyses (C5, C55, C83, C101, C118). Both evaluations support these findings as key contributions. OpenEval notes some uncertainty about developmental effects due to limited studies, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm the moderator findings including age, spindle type, and channel location effects.

Agreement on methodological limitations in the literature (C109-C111). Both evaluations accept these observational findings about reporting practices and transparency issues. Peer reviewers implicitly acknowledge these concerns through comments about Bayesian methods being 'less transparent.'

Agreement on memory type moderation findings (C98-C99). Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval notes limited sample sizes require cautious interpretation, while peer reviewers accept memory type as a key moderator without expressing concerns about the differential phase vs. strength predictions.

Strong disagreement on main conclusions (C6, C119). OpenEval finds conclusions supported by consistent evidence across analyses, noting small effect sizes as a caveat. Peer reviewers explicitly challenge the 'general physiological mechanism' conclusion, stating effect sizes are too small (< 0.10) to support such broad claims.

Partial agreement on SP amplitude findings (C85-C86, C116). Both evaluations support the findings about variability and specificity. However, peer reviewers express confusion about including amplitude measures since they don't directly measure coupling, though they don't challenge the results themselves.

Agreement on publication bias assessment (C90). Both evaluations accept the finding of no publication bias. OpenEval treats this as supporting robustness of results, and peer reviewers accept it without challenge as validating the effect size estimates.

Both address small effect sizes (C117). OpenEval treats this as an appropriate limitation acknowledgment common in neuroscience meta-analyses. Peer reviewers (R2) incorporate this concern more critically, using it to question whether effects support broad mechanistic conclusions.
